title: About fifteen million
hookLine: Jews today live mostly in Israel and North America, with communities worldwide

cards: Some prayers need a minyan, a quorum, so someone at the door has to count heads. And in some synagogues, the person counting won't say one, two, three. Some say, not one, not two, not three.
Some count by the words of a verse, one word per person. It sounds like a quirk. It's actually a very old instinct: be careful about counting people like objects.
Keep that in mind, because today's title is a number, and an enormous one: about fifteen million.

teach.h: COUNT THE COINS, NOT THE HEADS.
teach.b: The caution goes back to the Torah. When Moses is told to take a census, each person gives half a shekel of silver, so that no plague comes among them. The rabbis read it this way: count the coins, not the heads.
Later, when King David counts the people directly, the book of Samuel tells of a plague that follows. Behind both stories sits a conviction: a person is not a unit. And there's an older promise.

teach.h: COUNT THE STARS, IF YOU CAN.
teach.b: God takes Abraham outside at night and says: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." The point of that count is that you can't finish it.
Now the modern number: about fifteen million Jews in the world. It's an estimate, not a head count, because counting Jews raises real questions.

Orthodox and Conservative Judaism count a person Jewish through a Jewish mother or a conversion under Jewish law; Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism in North America also count a child of one Jewish parent who is raised Jewish.
Some people with Jewish roots don't call themselves Jewish; some who do, others wouldn't count. So the number comes with an asterisk. Where do they live?

Mostly in Israel and North America, then in communities around the world: France and Britain, Argentina and Brazil, Russia and Ukraine, South Africa, Australia, Morocco, India and elsewhere, some large, some a handful of families with one old synagogue.
Big enough to fill cities, small next to the stars. Each one a name, not a unit.

how: Some communities gathering a minyan avoid counting people by number, saying "not one, not two" or counting with the words of a verse; population estimates are made by demographers, who note that the answer depends on who is counted.

games.q: you're at the synagogue door, and you need to know if there are enough for a minyan. how do you count?

games.why: some communities count without numbers, an old caution from the Torah's census and King David's story: a person is not a unit.

practice: Name the people who make up your community, a congregation, a family, a team, a street, not with numbers but one by one, each with a face or one thing they do. Notice who comes easily and who you almost forgot.
It's a count where every one is a person.

wordCard.voice: Minyan. The quorum needed for some prayers, and the old instinct behind it: count the coins, not the heads, a care that holds even for the fifteen million Jews alive today. Today's word.
